speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the next few days the Government of Canada will be making important decisions on a new comprehensive native claims policy. This is an opportunity to establish a more productive and mutually beneficial relationship between the aboriginal peoples and all Canadians.
The new policy must affirm aboriginal rights. It must enable the aboriginal peoples to protect and enhance their cultures. It must allow them to have decision-making authority over their own lives, lands, and resources. Self-government must be a part of the new policy.
These are the essential elements, the reasonable and just accommodations which the Government must make if it is serious about making the aboriginal peoples partners in our great Canadian Confederation.

subsubtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE NEGOTIATIONS-POSITION OF LIBERAL PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the confusion and disarray among the Liberals on the importance of the freer trade talks continue to grow and spread.
There is the Leader who says: "It is no good but the talks must go on". Then there is the Hon. Member for Winnipeg- Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) who says: "No way. We are fence builders".
That confusion was compounded when the marketing vicepresident of Canada's largest Great Lakes shipping group, the Canada Steamship Lines, called for a common Shipping Act and the putting of U.S. shipping protectionism on the table of trade talks. Then came the well-known Liberal leadership contender, Paul Martin Jr., president of the same shipping company, who told a Liberal fund raising dinner in St. Catharines a few days ago that the free trade talks with the United States are not the answer.
No wonder the rank and file Liberals look like lost sheep wandering around in the wilderness without a shepherd.

subsubtopic: HONDURAS-REPORTED ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRA BASES BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of all the countries in South America, Honduras receives the most development aid from Canada. It receives almost $40 million a year. Considering this, Canadians must be very concerned about the growing militarization of Honduras. Today's Globe and Mail reported that the United States plans to establish Contra bases on Honduran islands off the coast of Nicaragua.
The Contra war is an anti-development war. The Contras have targeted teachers, doctors, nurses, and other development workers for murder and kidnapping.
If Honduras continues to be used as a military base to destroy development in Nicaragua, Canadians must ask about the value of our development assistance. Canada must protect the integrity of its development program by protesting to both the United States and Honduras against this crude attempt to force Nicaragua back into colonial status.

subsubtopic: HEADQUARTERS OF FUTURE CANADIAN AEROSPACE AGENCY
speechtext:
This week, Mr. Speaker, I asked that the Canadian aerospace agency be headquartered in my riding. Indeed the riding of Longueuil has all facilities to accommodate this agency whose establishment will be announced in the near future. My riding already has the skilled labour force needed in this field, not to mention an industrial and transport infrastructure which is second to none and ranks among the most efficient. Longueuil and Greater Montreal are ideally suited to the needs of the aerospace industry. Earlier this morning the Government decided to

October 31, 1986
award the F-18 maintenance contract, further acknowledgement that the Montreal region is best for aeronautical and aerospace projects.
Establishing the Canadian aerospace agency in Longueuil is bound to revive the local economy, especially so if the agency's mandate is to oversee the applied research related to this new technology. The agency will also reinforce our sectorial economy development policy.

Mr. Speaker, in the Throne Speech at the opening of this session of Parliament the Government said that special emphasis will be given to diversifying the economic base of western Canada. Prior to this in my own region we had the cancellation of the NRC research station, the VIA maintenance base, and many of the transportation aid programs. Now we have the statement made by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) that a western Canadian consortium is not capable of undertaking technology transfer in the interests of Canada. This is the effective program of economic development that the Government is offering to diversify the base of western Canada. Instead we have the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) saying that we are giving aid to farmers. This aid program is going to be distributed across the country.
The real question we have to ask is this. When is the Government going to understand that in order for western Canada to realize its economic potential it must have federal investment to enable it to develop its scientific, technological and industrial base. All the Government has done up until now is reduce, eliminate, subtract, and eviscerate that base. It is time that the Government understood that western Canada demands its fair share.

subsubtopic: NOVA SCOTIA LIBERAL PARTY-ADVICE ON ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OF HALIFAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out to all Atlantic Canadians that we in the P.C. Party are competely opposed to the current Liberal thinking as expressed at its annual meeting in Nova Scotia this past weekend.
The Liberal Party of Nova Scotia, short of ideas, sought the advice of National Sea President, Gordon Cummings, and of Bank of Nova Scotia Vice-President, Peter John Nicholson.
The Liberals were advised to concentrate economic development in Halifax at the expense of the rest of the Atlantic region. The idea is to turn Halifax into another Toronto. This may be the type of advice that the Liberals of Nova Scotia are seeking. These corporate people in their ivory towers will have a hard time justifying these ideas to the entrepreneurs of Middleton or the fish plant owners of Yarmouth. If the policy of the Liberal Party is to stifle business development in 99 per cent of the Atlantic region, I would like to state very emphatically that I am glad I am not a Liberal.

subsubtopic: LYELL ISLAND-PROTECTION OF HAIDA PEOPLE FROM LOGGING OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, less than a century ago over 90 per cent of the Haida population on the Queen Charlotte Islands perished from small pox and other diseases introduced by the white population. Thousands of Haida men, women, and children died in the South Moresby area in a few short months in the mid-1880s.
Yesterday the federal Government made it clear that a cash offer is on the table to compensate fully the loggers, communities and forest companies for the cutting rights on Lyell Island and South Moresby. The Haida have returned to Lyell Island and they are erecting a long house at Windy Bay. They have made it clear that these lands are their country, their spirit, their past and their future, and that they will be preserved.
Yesterday the federal Government warned of violence and even death if the logging continues. Mr. Speaker, the logging continues at the request of Premier Vander Zalm. Today the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) must call his friend and avert disaster. The process that will lead to the possible death of Haidas, loggers or others, must be stopped.

In recent weeks, Mr. Speaker, we have been witnessing a rather peculiar phenomenon. Our Liberal Opposition colleagues are adamantly opposed to the construction of a prison in Port-Cartier in the riding of Manicouagan because, they claim, it will cost a little bit more. Apparently, Mr. Speaker, they would have us believe that every time the Government is prepared to spend a little bit more money to create jobs in regions which are far removed from major urban centres we ought to forget about it and
October 31, 1986

totally ignore these people who are up against high unemployment and its many attendant problems.
If this is true, Mr. Speaker, does the logic of the Liberal Party imply that we ought to neglect or simply abandon Canadians who happen to live far away from major cities, in regions where we might have to spend more generously to spur the economy?
Our Opposition colleagues would be well advised to reconsider their funnel-like approach to regional disparities in this vast country of ours, otherwise many Canadian men and women might make them regret it.

subsubtopic: LYELL ISLAND-NEGOTIATIONS URGED TO STOP LOGGING OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, South Moresby, in particular Lyell Island, continues to be the focal point of conflict between Western Forests Products and the Haida Nation. Yesterday in the House the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) said that "the Government of Canada would be very predisposed toward sitting down with" Western Forests Products "to negotiate the value of the timber licences and to reasonably compensate the company-".
The Minister left unanswered the legitimate question of why negotiations to stop the logging have not begun. If there is a disposition to negotiate, why are negotiations not yet under way in light of this near-crisis situation? I urge the Minister to proceed with all possible speed, because the situation is serious, and to demonstrate the Government's commitment to native rights in South Moresby and throughout Canada.

subsubtopic: VIDEO CAMPAIGN TO COMBAT DRUG ABUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the video messages which the Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher) unveiled yesterday are proof of the Government's desire to urge Canadian youth to resist drugs. Drug abuse, including alcohol abuse, does untold damage to our young people. Drugs sap the potential of young lives and can cause irreparable damage.
Along with drug enforcement must come drug education. We must do more to impress upon Canadians, especially youth, that taking illegal drugs is socially and personally unacceptable. We must reduce the demand for drugs, and we must do it early.
Professional and amateur athletes represent an excellent way to reach youth with a message to which they will listen. Athletes are role models and an inspiration to Canadian youth. When they talk, young people listen. The co-operative spirit between Government and professional sport means that everyone wins. Through continued support and hard work we shall reduce the demand for drugs among Canadian youth.

subsubtopic: AWARDING OFCF-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT MAINTENANCE CONTRACT TO CANADAIR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, only one hour ago the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) announced that the F-18 maintenance contract is being awarded to Canadair despite the fact that the Bristol bid was less expensive and that government people consider it to be of higher technological value. The reason of technological transfer given by the President of the Treasury Board was not even considered in the evaluation system of government officials.
This points out the problem we have with our tendering and bidding system. It is very important that citizens and corporations of Canada believe that they will be dealt with equitably in the tendering system. If the Government is going to award a contract on a basis other than price or technical evaluation, then that should be stated at the outset. It is a matter not only of the integrity of the bidding system, but of the integrity of the Government itself.

subsubtopic: RECEIPT OF CF-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT MAINTENANCE CONTRACT BY CANADAIR-IMPACT ON MONTREAL REGION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today, the people of Montreal must be both proud and disappointed.
The Government's decision reflects honourably, first of all, on the workers at Canadair, the Canadair Survival Committee chaired by Mr. Cherry, all the members of the Board of Trade of Montreal, and on Robert Bourassa who managed to force the Government to make up for the mistakes it made in Quebec. Today, I think Montreal has reason to be proud and to rejoice.
It is too bad, however that Quebecers have to set up a survival committee and come all the way to Ottawa just to get their fair share.

October 31, 1986
Oral Questions

The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development has joined the Auditor General in publicly praising the Government for its efforts in managing the public purse and the deficit. I commend the Government for its commitment and efforts to curb public expenditures. Guidelines for economic renewal have been stated, such as tax reform, enhanced trade, and increased employment. We are on the road to economic recovery and the foundation has been laid for sustained growth. Saskatoonians, and Canadians in general, will benefit from a Government which is prepared to face tough decisions related to reduced expenditures, duplication, and waste.
When you look at the Liberal Party you can see the flaws in their own financial management. At the time of the 1984 election they borrowed money and were in debt to the tune of $2.5 million. Now officials claim they must raise almost $22 million in the next two years to pay off the debt and get through another federal election without going into the hole. Shame on the Liberals who mismanaged the public purse and who cannot practise fiscal responsibility.

subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF HON. RICHARD FRENCH, MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS OF THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: PRESENCE IN GALLERY OF HON. RICHARD FRENCH, MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS OF THE PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext: Order! I would like to draw the attention of the House to the presence in our gallery of the Hon. Richard French, Minister of Communications of the Province of Quebec.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State for Immigration. Under the immigration levels announced yesterday the Government, for the third year in a row, froze at
45,000	the number of immigrants who can be reunited with their families in Canada. Why did the Minister choose to ignore the strong recommendation of the parliamentary
committee for an increase in the family class under our immigration rules?

Mr. Speaker, as I indicated when I responded to the standing committee report, I was able to respond favourably to almost all of their recommendations. There was only one I disagreed with. The five recommendations dealing with the assisted family and assisted relative class, which I described as the most exicting and far-reaching, needed more consultation and thought. subtopic: INQUIRY WHY SUFFICIENT PERSONNEL NOT FORESEEN TO PROCESS IMMIGRATION APPLICATIONS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: INQUIRY WHY SUFFICIENT PERSONNEL NOT FORESEEN TO PROCESS IMMIGRATION APPLICATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister created false expectations when he promised to increase immigration to Canada without providing the personnel required to process immigration applications, especially for family reunification.
Why did the Minister not provide sufficient personnel to process immigration applications, especially for family reunification?

subtopic: INQUIRY WHY SUFFICIENT PERSONNEL NOT FORESEEN TO PROCESS IMMIGRATION APPLICATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the quality and intensity of the work of all Members of Parliament who went around the world and provided me with an excellent report on procedures and practices gave me a good indication of the ways I can improve and cut out a lot of the bureaucratic red tape and ease the entry of immigrants to Canada. I have also looked at the quality of service in our country. We are going to look at state of the art technology, and the procedures and practices which have been in place for years and which we cannot rationalize. When we do all those things and become more efficient and cut down a lot of the struggles and frustrations people have been going through, we are going to be able to bring a lot more people into this country with the same resources.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister says that he followed the recommendations of the committee. He ignored one of the more important recommendations. Another one that he ignored is a change in the evaluation system for immigrants to allow more points for those people who have family members in Canada. Why did the Minister not accept that recommendation so as to facilitate the reunification of families and allow Canadians already in the country to have their family members join them here?
October 31, 1986

Mr. Speaker, one thing is very clear. We have heard and understood the frustrations and what the communities have been going through. In the levels that I announced yesterday, we added some 32 new categories of independent skills in which immigrants do not need a relative or do not need a certified job offer in their pocket. While we withdrew 12, the 20 additional categories show our willingness to make movement in those areas.
We said that in order to open the assisted family class and assisted relative class we would have to understand the full implication and do so in consultation with the community, the provinces, the private and public sector, and indeed with Members of Parliament. That is what we will be doing. Furthermore, an indepth study under the Minister of National Health and Welfare is already under way, with the participation of my Department. We look forward to the results.

subsubtopic: AWARDING OF CF-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT MAINTENANCE CONTRACT-TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER FACTOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Supply and Services. In making the announcement of the decision on the CF-18 maintenance contract this morning, the President of the Treasury Board confirmed that Bristol Aerospace had the lowest price and lowest bid. When the original tenders were announced, price, not the question of technology transfer, was considered to be the primary criterion. When did the change take place? Why did you make the change, and why was that not part of the total submission so that all the companies would have an equal chance in that kind of application?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: AWARDING OF CF-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT MAINTENANCE CONTRACT-TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER FACTOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we had two excellent contenders at the final moment, through the bidding process. They were very close on technical merit and on cost. We looked very closely at the issue of technology transfer because it is an important issue for the country. The Government had a choice, and it made a very deliberate choice to favour Canadair because we felt that the downstsream technology transfer could be better done through the existing facilities of Canadair than by the competing consortium because Canadair is a producer of aircraft as well as being in the maintenance business. The bids were close and it was because of that overriding factor that the contract went to Canadair.

Mr. Speaker, this being Halloween, it looks like it is a case of trick and treat. I suggest that we have to ask some serious questions about the way the process was handled.
Oral Questions
Without looking at the end result, the fact is that when the original tenders were put forward and the applications were sought, the question was basically one of the lowest bidder for that contract. Now that the rules have been changed in midstream, is it not proper that the Government should have made that very clear to those excellent submissions that were made so that there would not now be the suggestion that in fact the real question was one of interference, not one of confidence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, there was no interference of any kind. Second, it was clearly indicated in the original bids that the Government, as in all bids-which the Hon. Member's deskmate can confirm-is never bound to the lowest bid. That is clearly outlined in those submissions. However, my colleague raises an interesting point and one that I would like to address seriously in the House.
Stating all of the national concerns that we may have in making a final decision is something that we would certainly want to consider in future requests for submissions. That has never been done before and my hon. friend has raised a serious issue that we would be happy to consider. However, I still stand fast by my word that this contract, on an economic and financial basis and for the future of Canada, was given to the best consortium that made a bid.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. On February 12 in the newspaper La Presse, someone from the Prime Minister's Office clearly indicated that Canadair would obtain the contract. According to the newspaper, a source near the Prime Minister had said that Canadair could virtually rely on getting the contract.
The very next day in Winnipeg, the Minister of National Health and Welfare was quoted as saying: "I just know that from our Manitoba perspective, things will be okay". The Minister followed that up by another extraordinary statement. I hold the headline in my hand. The Minister of National Health and Welfare said in Manitoba he was confident the CF-18 contract would land in Manitoba. In a decision as important as this in terms of its regional reception, does the Prime Minister think it is appropriate for Ministers of the Crown to go around the country building up false expectations, with different things being said in different parts of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I think, not unlike some other matters in the past, this contract has brought about a fair amount of comment from Members of Parliament and people who are not Members of Parliament. I do not think that is to be unexpected.

October 31, 1986
Oral Questions
I suppose in a country as diverse as ours that is something which has taken place and will take place in the future. I do not think there was anything untoward said in any of those cases. I think the reasons provided by the President of the Treasury Board indicate that the award was made in the national interest.

Mr. Speaker, I find the Prime Minister's answer extraordinary. Is he saying it is his perception, not that of Members of Parliament, backbenchers, or even members of the Opposition, that Ministers of the Crown who will be involved in the decision themselves ought to go around the country in future acting as cheerleaders for their regions and leaving their regions with the expectation that an important decision which will be made is going to come down on their side? Does that not sow confusion in the country instead of promoting national unity which a Cabinet should be about?

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I will consult the statements my hon. friend has in front of him from some months ago. I would be happy to take a look at them. I did not hear that anyone was trying to provoke disunity in any way. Cabinet officers clearly from time to time are called upon to make comments on impending decisions, which in no way violates their commitment to objective consideration. I think that is probably a fair statement.
I, along with my hon. friend, recognize that from time to time certain issues will challenge national unity. Even with the best faith in the world, from time to time in Canada issues will arise which will be placed in that context. Decisions such as this are made with a sense of fairness and a realization of that historic difficulty in Canada, which is why I ask for the support of my hon. friend in this kind of decision which was clearly made in the national Canadian interest.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT MINISTERS NOT MAKE CONFLICTING STATEMENTS PRIOR TO AWARDING OF CONTRACTS
REQUEST THAT MINISTERS NOT MAKE CONFLICTING STATEMENTS PRIOR TO AWARDING OF CONTRACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the President of the Treasury Board in his announcement today said the decision was made in the national interest and I clearly hope that was the case. Will the Prime Minister give us assurances that, before any other major decision of this kind is made, he will give instructions to his Cabinet Ministers not to go around the country saying different things in different regions creating expectations that he knows inevitably will be frustrated in part because all regions, in a decision like this, cannot perceive themselves simultaneously to be winners? Will he give us that assurance?

speechtext:

a total sense of objectivity and a degree of dispassion in regard to their regions and their electors, of which they are from time to time incapable. I understand that. Member that all members of the Government deliberated in a spirit of fairness and openness and arrived at a decision to complement the national interest. 1982 your Government eliminated the independent skills-

subsubtopic: AWARDING OF CF-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT MAINTENANCE CONTRACT-TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER FACTOR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. If technology transfer was the basis for the decision with regard to the CF-18 contract, why was it not a part of the original 75-member panel process? Why were the rules of the game changed at the end of the game in the ninth inning? How does the Minister square his claim that technology transfer was the basis for the decision with the fact that the technology transfer was left out of the original panel process?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
subsubtopic: AWARDING OF CF-18 FIGHTER AIRCRAFT MAINTENANCE CONTRACT-TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER FACTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I have already answered the question. It is a little difficult to enhance my previous answer. Perhaps we should have said that in the original bids. I have instrmed my officials to talk with the officials of the Department of Supply and Services to ensure that we might mention that type of thing. In one case we felt that there was a compelling argument that technology for Canadians would be transferred more effectively than in the other case, and we opted for that choice. We had a choice and we made it. We stand by it.
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same Minister. I note that the Minister has just admitted that he changed the rules at the end of the game.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, is the Minister now ready to make public all the documents, including the report of the original panel on this bidding process, particularly in light of the doubt that has been cast on the bidding process and in light of the questions that have been raised about changing the rules of the game? speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to tell my hon. colleague that there was no change in the bidding process in any way, shape or form, at any time, in any contract-
Just the evaluation!

There was no change in any way in the bidding process. It is well known that when we enter into a competitive bidding process and the bids are within 10 per cent of each other there are questions of national interest and so on that can be brought in perhaps to balance the scale in favour of one or another. Second, there is no doubt cast on the decision. It is a decision which was made in the national interest with respect to technology transfer. I wish to assure my hon. colleague that I will make all relevant information available, as long as it does not contravene the normal practices which are in place to maintain the confidential nature of information given to us by competitors. If they are willing to make the information available, then I am more than happy to give the Hon. Member all the information. This is a decision which is good for the country, and I am willing to stand by it. I will be happy to give the Hon. Member the information.

Since the Government refused to identify them and left the matter in the hands of Mr. Justice Estey as of October 4, 1985, and since the Estey Report is silent on the

matter, will the Minister now undertake to release the names of those uninsured depositors so that the taxpayers may know where their money went?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too have a question on the subject of the Estey Commission Report and on the pay-out of close to $1 billion to uninsured depositors upon which the Government decided but which was not dealt with adequately in the Estey Commission Report. Since
the Estey Commission made it clear that the failure of the two banks was due to their improvident lending practices in the early part of the 1980s and perhaps earlier, and since the information provided by auditors to depositors for their guidance was wrong but that was a normal commercial risk, can the Minister now explain why the taxpayer has to pay $1 billion when it is clear that those depositors took commercial risks and they should have paid for that themselves?

subsubtopic: ESTEY COMMISSION REPORT-COST OF COMPENSATING UNINSURED DEPOSITORS

Member for Rosemont seemed to think that transport meant trips abroad, while the Hon. This is a clear demonstration of this Government's incompetence in the area of transportation. I must say that the only things which have worked well in that Department are the political appointments, because the most massive and scandalous political appointments over the past two years under this Government have been made by the former Minister of Transport and his officials. Transportation in Canada has always been and must remain a major instrument of economic development. This country has been established and developed thanks to our railway network and has witnessed a significant economic expansion from coast to coast brought about by the construction and operation of airports and seaports. Madam Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to speak for a few minutes, but before giving Canadians the information I have prepared, I would like to suggest to the Hon. Madam Speaker, I intend to address the Government's priorities in the transport field. The Government's highest
priority is surely to guarantee the safety of our transportation network. We cannot and will not tolerate any compromise for the sake of achieving other Government objectives in this sector. In pursuing this objective, the Government has taken some important initiatives with respect to our various transportation modes, and it continues to do so. Last year, Parliament approved a number of amendments to the Aeronautics Act, which gave Canada its best legislation on aviation security in 60 years. The regulations on the transportation of hazardous goods were adopted last year, and they are now being implemented with the full co-operation of all provinces. After consultation with the provinces, we also reached agreement on a uniform national safety code for the trucking industry.
Amendments to the Canada Shipping Act, designed to improve marine safety, were tabled in the House last spring and will be reintroduced for debate. As for the railways, we have had consultations with all parties concerned, prior to drafting amendments to the Railway Act that will promote the use of advanced technology.
The Government's commitment to economic reform remains firm. Very shortly, we shall be tabling the new National Transportation Act and the accompanying Motor Vehicle Transportation Act. Except for a few minor technical changes, these Bills will be identical to those tabled last June. We trust they will be considered without delay and given the attention they deserve.
The last major review of our national transportation legislation took place nearly 25 years ago. The Hon. Member for Papineau said earlier that his Government had done a great deal for transportation in this country, but it has been 25 years since they or any government even touched this legislation. In 1961, Madam Speaker, the MacPherson Royal Commission of Inquiry published a report on transport that was to form the basis for the National Transportation Act passed in 1967. Since then, the sector has developed and matured considerably. The trucking industry is buoyant, and the railways have concentrated their operations in bulk commodity transport.
Air transport has trebled and never before have such comprehensive services been available in this sector.
Intermodal transport services have expanded and the needs of shippers have diversified. The number of Canadians who prefer train or bus travel has declined, and the automobile remains the favourite way to travel in Canada.
The 1967 National Transportation Act and other related statutes stem from a regulatory approach which is no longer acceptable. Such legislation were adopted when transport markets were considered as being underdeveloped and when carriers were deemed to need protection.
In short, Madam Speaker, over the past 20 years the previous Government took a paternalistic view of people involved in transportation, and we intend to steer a different
October 31, 1986

course altogether. Similarly, users are subject to undue control by regulatory agencies which decide for them how they should deal with carriers. Such regulations have stifled the competitive spirit and more often than not have led to higher rates and fewer services.
As the transportation sector expands, regulations ought to become more flexible and simpler to enable the industry to meet the ever changing needs of shippers and users alike. We should eliminate restrictions which thwart competitiveness and keep prices high, and then promote diversity and initiative. The regulations and the agency which implements them should be more flexible, more readily accessible to Canadians, less procedure-oriented.
Madam Speaker, when I was responsible for small business-in the Department of Industry, if you will-my provincial counterparts and I signed memorandums of agreement to reduce red tape and simplify procedures. We will take similar action in the transportation sector. We should encourage mediation and less formal dispute settlements. As stated in the November 8, 1984 document entitled "A New Direction for Canada: An Agenda for Economic Renewal", the current economic situation calls for the removal of barriers which stand in the way of growth and competitiveness in Canada's transport industry.
A fresh policy and a new legislative framework have become imperative if we are to face the realities of the 1980s, the 1990s and beyond, and if we aim at building a sound foundation which will enable us to meet the challenges and benefit from the opportunities of the next century.
The new legislation reflects the commitment of the Conservative Government to five principles. First, transportation safety is our number one priority and we cannot over emphasize it. As you will recall, Madam Speaker, whenever there is an announcement or a press conference regarding new transportation legislation or policies, security always is and still remains the priority. The Canadian transportation network must meet the needs of shippers and travellers. Trimmed down regulations which would reduce the intervention of the state would stimulate innovation and entrepreneurship. Greater reliance on competition and market forces will result in a decrease of unit costs, more competitive prices and a greater range of services for shippers and the Canadian public.
Canadians want a regulatory framework which is both open and accessible without being excessively slow and costly as is now the case.
Madam Speaker, the reforms contained in the new legislation represent a made-in-Canada policy. The existing legislation provides only one way of dealing with complaints by shippers, carriers or the public: an investigation by the Canadian Transport Commission, which can include a public hearing to determine whether the public interest is involved.
This procedure has been criticized by everyone as too costly, too slow and inappropriate for settling differences about prices or services between a shipper and a carrier, for instance.

New provisions taking into account the particular situation of transport in Canada are proposed so that private differences between shippers and carriers can be settled quickly and economically:
A mediation service provided by the National Transportation Agency at the request of the parties involved.
An arbitration procedure will be established to settle differences when mediation fails. The independent arbitrator appointed by the National Transportation Agency will be able to choose only between the final offer of the carrier and that of the shipper.
The new legislation will also include an amended and more effective investigation mechanism for the cases where the public interest is involved.
Upon a complaint being filed, the national transportation board will be empowered to investigate any actions, omissions or rates of a carrier that could harm the public interest.
The various needs of different areas of Canada have been taken into account by the previous Minister of Transport, the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), following many consultations held across the country, and also by the Standing Committee on Transport.
To give but two examples, the results speak for themselves. The national transport policy statement, on which the new national transportation board based its decisions, does recognize that transportation is the key to regional development, as this Government has indicated on a number of occasions. Regional development is one of our commitments, and transportation is the key to that development.
The regulations concerning air services in Northern Canada, which the Deputy Prime Minister referred to earlier, will include other criteria that will safeguard the public interest, namely the maintenance of essential air services at reasonable costs in difficult and precarious conditions.
In Southern Canada, where most Canadians live, this increased competition between air carriers will lead to better fares and to services that are better suited to passenger needs. Madam Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to rise on behalf of my Party to debate a motion that addresses a serious problem, to use its own words, in "frivolous ideological" terms.
The import of this motion is essentially to put all those federally-regulated means of transport in Canada out for debate. That is a worthy intent. The fashion in which it has been done does not reflect any credit on the movers of the motion. It is a fashion that suggests that we will have un dialogue de sourds, an interchange between two sides in terms of the failures of one and the achievements of the other. Into that debate 1 will attempt to inject, if I may make so bold, some measure of discussion of what the real problems in transport in Canada are, how they derive, and where the solutions may lie.
The motion that the Opposition has put forward covers almost every aspect of freight and passenger traffic in Canada. Reading the text of the motion, one could almost imagine that the Liberals had not been in power for a decade or held power for 17 of the last 20 years. Reality is different. Virtually everything that this motion complains about is the result of decisions taken, actions left undone or indeed done by the previous Liberal Governments. It is worthwhile to mention that while I have no cause or inclination to defend the Government, the fact is that many of the things that have happened in the area of transport over the past few years have their roots in the inaction or the budgetary shortcomings of the previous Liberal Government.
Airline deregulation began in the Ministry of Transport when the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) was Minister. He was pulling in people from right and left, overspending his budget by a factor of twice and breaking some of the rules which then constrained the salaries of his officials in order to gear up the public relations effort that went along with this. Presumably the Liberals are taking the position that their brand of regulation would not have gone as far as the present Government. Since the Government has passed no legislation of substance in this area up until now, it is clear where these trends and initiatives started. We must acknowledge that the idea of complete deregulation at the same time of all phases of federally-regulated transport in Canada is a folly which originates with this Government. I would dare to say that it is a folly which is encountering increasing resistance as the adverse consequences become evident. It is obvious that in the area of freight transportation, no matter how the freight is travelling, in a time when industry is suffering from low commodity prices, low returns on transport, and poor sales during this transition period, deregulation is being introduced at a time and in a fashion that can only aggravate some of the problems which now exist. We
have had contradictory statements from the Government and have not had it plain and clear as to the future role, if any, of the Canadian Transport Commission. The issue of safety is essential to an understanding of this debate and it is an essential part of the concern that all Members of Parliament should be demonstrating for Canadians. This means there will be a free-for-all in the transportation sector.

If we do such a thing, we will be rendering a disservice to our fellow Canadians. Equally from the Government's side, if we were to go around and say that safety will not and cannot be compromised, then we might miss the reality of some serious changes in the safety regime which may have unfortunate consequences for Canadians.
I am referring particularly to the matter of air travel safety and rail transportation safety. We have at last the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. My belief is that the preliminary implications of the CASB are very good. I would also point out that recent studies indicate that the regulations on fatigue in flying, principally pilot fatigue, are among the least effective in the world. They are not widely and strictly enforced in the manner that they should be. In many cases they do not provide for adequate recuperation for pilots before undertaking their next flight. Like most Members of the House, I read the aviation safety reports and the accident reports. I also read the reports of minor accidents. The number of cases in which pilot error is indicated should be a clear warning to the Government that there is something lacking in the present system. Also the lack of ability to enforce the existing safety regulations is something that should concern every Member of the House.
The operating rules for railways which have been enforced for many years by the Railway Transport Committee of the CTC were not regulations introduced on a whim or a caprice. They were introduced over a period of years or decades in response to perceived needs. To say-

As the Minister of State (Transport) (Mr. Bissonnette) said, we are going to get rid of all that red tape and even tear up the rule book-I'm not quite sure about the context-but I think we should not forget that this so-called red tape consists of regulations that are there for a very good reason, namely to ensure our safety.

We should look at those safety regulations. The Government must take the utmost care in discarding any one of those regulations.
Turning to the situation of rail freight under this Government, we have seen over the last couple of years a continuation of the trend toward job cuts. I am very glad to see the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner) sitting in the House. This is a matter that relates to the substance of this motion that I feel he should be taking up with his Department and on which he should be conducting a detailed scrutiny. When I read the press release on immigration levels I see that three categories of railway workers and the category of airline pilots, are designated as categories in which Canada has a shortage by virtue of being awarded 10 points in the immigration regulations. I cannot believe that that is so. In my riding many railway workers have been laid off or have been bumped to other parts of the system. Many pilots in Canada are unable to obtain employment, even though in some cases they possess the highest qualifications that our licencing system allows. The idea that we are effectively telling people in other countries that Canada has a shortage of people to fill those jobs is, to my mind, not only a slap in the face for those Canadians in those occupations who are unemployed, but is also cruelly deceiving those people who might come to this country under the assumption that such jobs are available.
We have already gone into the matter of privatization and the problems that this is causing particularly in terms of the CNR. I would be surprised to hear anyone on the government side deny the loss of employment that has occurred in the maintenance, the engineering, and the repair functions of the CNR. I am surprised that CN is not looking at those proposed job cuts with more appreciation for its potential liability should there be an accident which can be directly traced to deficient standards or defective maintenance. I believe the savings in eliminating these maintenance and overhaul jobs would look small compared to the possible liability involved in the companies being sued by someone who suffered an accident because of a failure of equipment resulting from lack of maintenance. Cabooseless trains is an example of the same problem. What will be the legal position of CN or CP in an accident where the injured party could claim that the lack of a caboose was a contributing cause to an accident? We have also heard in the last two months complaints from railway pensioners. In any debate on our transport system it is entirely legitimate that we raise those concerns. In many cases these people have given their whole working life to the railway system and now, because of a lack of indexation or inflation adjustment, they find their retirement incomes are totally inadequate. In examining the rail sector I think we have to harken back to reports issued some years ago which show the degree to which the railways' infrastructure costs and those of other modes of transportation are subsidized. If ever those costs were factored in to the cost of the transportation network as a whole, we know the rail mode would look a lot better than it does today.

Turning to air transport, the airport management strategy of this Government seems to have nothing to it but cut, cut, cut. The Government wants to slough off the responsibility for airports to municipal authorities. It seeks to cut back drastically the subsidies to municipal airports by something like 30 per cent next year. Where is it going to end? Are we going to have a national transportation system or are we going to have airports run individually by the municipalities, with a resulting lack of co-ordination? Perhaps the Government feels there is a better way to do things but it must realize that some airports will not be able to continue without these subsidies. It would also be unreasonable for anyone in this debate to talk about airports without mentioning the expenditures, some of them useful but much of them needless, on airports in the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) riding. All Members of the House should be interested in this comparison. In Kenora-Rainy River there are presently 32 active airports, only four of which receive assistance from Transport Canada. The number of passengers passing through those airports far exceeds those of airports which are much less active but which have received capital works such as runway extensions for which there was no operational argument to justify them other than the need for paying someone to put down paving which probably has not had a wheel on it yet.

Madam Speaker, I would also like to comment briefly on the situation in Canada's shipyards, and especially in the Province of Quebec. It seems that today, about 70 per cent of skilled workers in Canada shipyards are unemployed, and this Government-need we bring this up again-met with the president of one of the shipyards to look at the future of the industry in Quebec, which is clearly a conflict of interest situation. On March 26, it was announced that a $130- million contract would be awarded to Versatile Davie for the construction of a super ferry for CN Marine, now Marine Atlantic Inc. It has now been six months and nothing has materialized yet. Why? The Government should explain, Madam Speaker.

I would like to turn now to the situation of VIA Rail. That corporation was established by the previous Liberal Government with great fanfare and shortly thereafter left in orphan status. The present state of affairs is that the companies dedicated personnel, particularly the operating personnel, are doing their best with ancient equipment. The Government announced several times that there would be new engines and new rail cars to replace the creeking 30 year old and 40 year old equipment on VIA Rail. Again-

As in the case of the super ferry, except that this has been going on for a much longer period, nothing has been done. There have been no announcements whatsoever.

The CN and CP charges, which never seem to have been submitted to a proper examination by an outside authority, are of course dragging VIA Rail down into a deeper deficit position. What the people of this country are looking for in the matter of VIA Rail is simple honesty. The Government should either say it will cure VIA Rail, or stand up with some dignity and belief in its principles and say it will kill VIA Rail. It makes no sense, from either a management or political point of view, to keep VIA Rail in this state of limbo. The Government has to be clear on where it stands on the future of VIA Rail. The uncertainty is far worse than any precise move the Government could make, be it positive or negative.
Finally, I would like to talk about some of the consequences within my own riding which flow from the Government's drift and lack of initiative. We have had lay-offs in the divisional points of Sioux Lookout, Rainy River and Kenora. We have seen lay-offs of CN personnel in Fort Frances, not just in the running trades or the equipment department, but also in the maintenance-of-way and other ancilliary areas. We have seen contracting out of bunkhouse operations and of course our railway workers have faced the threat of job elimination, which is surely at the end of the agenda in the cabooseless train hearings.
We know, in spite of the transitional provisions, which I think were indeed wise, concerning deregulation of air traffic, that airlines in northern Ontario are basically on a hit list of the majors. In the last couple of days we have seen Air Canada moving to take over Air Ontario and Austin Air. We know that in the past this has led to predatory practices directed at the smaller airlines and their elimination. My constituents fear that this will happen again.
The Government has continually stalled on the matter of extending the Loran C network to cover the whole of Canada. I have risen on more than one occasion and pointed out to the Government the very useful improvements in navigation and therefore in air safety available through installation of this system. Indeed, within the last couple of days it has come to my attention that the American Government may be interested in the construction of a Loran C station in Canada which would also improve coverage in the U.S. because of unique locational factors. The Government should be grasping at that sort of possibility instead of ignoring it. For the Government to say that the global satellite positioning system is an effective substitute is to ignore the realities of the difficulties in the United States space program and to ignore the responsibility for creating jobs and improving air safety in Canada in this decade rather than waiting for the next. In conclusion, the Government must give the entire area of transport much more attention.

Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to the Hon. Member's speech on this motion. He mentioned what a good system the Loran C is for navigation,
for aircraft as well as ships. The Canadian Owners & Pilots Association publishes a monthly newsletter. They qualified what the Hon. Member said about the Loran C coverage. The newsletter says that by 1990 the United States will have coverage for the entire continental U.S. Saskatchewan is a preferred site for such a station.
In the same newsletter there is a little note with regard to the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mulroney) riding of Manicouagan. It says:
According to press reports, the Right Honourable Brian Mulroney has announced that ILS installations, costing $7 1/2 million, are to be made at airports within the boundaries of his constituency of Manicouagan. It was pointed out to us that his particular riding is bathed in marine Loran C signals which may be used by aircraft having functioning Loran C receivers to conduct non-precision approaches at no additional cost for ground transmitters.
Is the Hon. Member aware of this? When Hon. Members have asked for a few dollars to create part-time employment in their ridings, members of the Government have indicated that we are extremely short of funds. Is the Member aware that this is occurring in the Prime Minister's riding? Does he think that those dollars may be better spent elsewhere? This is what the Canadian Owners & Pilots Association are pointing out to us.

Madam Speaker, I must thank my hon. colleague for his question, which I could not have phrased better myself. Members on the government side may not appreciate the utility of the availability of the Loran C signals in the riding of Manicouagan or in most coastal districts of Canada. As reported in the newsletter from which my hon. colleague quoted, the use of such a system enables a pilot to split the numbers. In other words, he may land accurately at the end of a runway through the use of that navigational system only. I understand that a company in the United States uses that system to keep track of its delivery vehicles within a city. This is a system of great accuracy. That is of obvious benefit to non-marine areas of Canada. Pilots in central Canada could derive great use from it.
The Hon. Member's question illustrates very well the double standard which the Government applies with regard to the funding of projects. Money is available to gild the lilies in the Prime Minister's riding. A good system is already in place there, yet there is $7.5 million available to enhance the instrument landing system when neither accuracy nor safety is available in many other parts of Canada.
This is not a criticism which I make lightly, Madam Speaker, but I thought it was the most disgraceful manipulation that I have ever seen when the Prime Minister produced a widow from his riding to say that she would not be a widow if this system had existed previously. That is disgraceful because many people from remote ridings in Canada would be able to make the same claim and twist the public's collective heartstrings in that very way. For the Prime Minister to suggest by implication-

Madam Speaker, I am rather surprised to hear the Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry), who seems to be in cahoots with the Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), saying that the Government seems to be forgetting about the safety standards which protect travellers. He made very little reference to the Aeronautics Act which was amended last June. I would like to put a couple of points on the record.
The Aeronautics Act provided for an independent civil aviation tribunal system to be created to hear and determine appeals from penalties assessed by Transport Canada quickly, fairly and informally. Challenges could be made to suspension or cancellation of a licence, an assessment of fines or refusal to renew a licence. Doctors and optometrists will be required to report conditions of patients holding licences who may have medical problems which could affect flight safety. Licence holders will be required to identify themselves to any attending physician or optometrist and are deemed to consent to the disclosure of medical information.
Coupled with that are the safety measures in our airports in which each of us take part every week. There are X-ray machines in place. Since last October baggage has not been allowed to precede a passenger on international flights. By next year this safety measure will be in place on domestic flights. There is now more RCMP presence in the airports in addition to the regular security personnel.
In light of all the things which the Hon. Member himself has seen taking place in the past year and the various regulations which have been put into effect, would he not agree that the setting of standards and their diligent enforcement is a logical means of protecting the public interest? Instead of telling people that the Government is doing nothing, why does he not report that which has actually happened and been put in place through law?

Madam Speaker, I must thank the Hon. Member for the opportunity to address those concerns. He is talking about security. I did not have the opportunity to discuss airport security in my speech. Although the methods that are being used are cumbersome and irritating to many travellers, I agree that they make a great deal of sense in view of the world-wide increase in terrorism against aviation. In Canada we have mercifully experienced only one instance, although that was indeed a terrible instance.
1 was talking about regulations and the ability to enforce them. While the improvement of an appeal system for people accused of offences against the Aeronautics Act is desirable, 1 cannot see how that, in itself, will enhance safety.
The Hon. Member does make some legitimate points about security and a good point about the appeal system. However,

these do not address the safety concerns. He will know that the number of near miss incidents reported by air traffic controllers in Canada has risen by an uncomfortable amount in spite of the measures he is talking about.

Madam Speaker, I want to make two points. The opposition Parties appear to be denouncing deregulation, yet every one of these incidents that have been mentioned have happened under a regulated society. How can they blame these incidents on something that has not yet come into force? It is beyond me and simply does not make sense because these happened under a regulated society.
My second point concerns truckers. For many years regulation has been the downfall of our trucking industry. In fact, I am surprised that we have a national trucking industry in Canada at all. If a trucker from Alberta wants to haul goods into or through Saskatchewan, he first must get a permit in Alberta which costs approximately $1,000 and then get another permit in Saskatchewan for another $ 1,500 or $2,000. If he wants to go through Manitoba, Ontario, and Quebec, he must pay another $2,000 or $3,000 in each province. In other words, these regulations have created ten separate states in Canada, and in order for a trucker to haul beef from Alberta to Montreal, he had to go through the United States. We had to make arrangements with the Americans for our truckers to go through the United States. I wish I had more time because these regulations are destroying the trucking industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I apologize to the Speaker and my colleagues for not being in my chair. However, I had been summoned by a page.
What is most disconcerting about having to be recalled in such a way is that not only have I upset Madam Speaker and my colleagues in the House, who 1 know were waiting with bated breath for my comments, but I find myself rising to speak having just been the beneficiary of a kind gesture from Members opposite. You do not know how it pains my heart, therefore, to have to proceed with the comments I must, in good conscience, make.
Today we have set aside a period of time in the House to debate what is really an urgent and pressing matter in this country. It is the insidious, slow and almost invisible manner in which the Government of Canada has completely changed the way in which Canadians and, more importantly, the Government views the role of transportation in our nation.
I believe it is important to look at the history of transportation in Canada. From the days of John A. Macdonald, that great Conservative Prime Minister who I am sure Members opposite will applaud-
Hear, hear!

They are so predictable, Madam Speaker. From the days of John A. Macdonald, transportation has always been a vehicle for building this country. John A. Macdonald did not propose and support the notion of building railways from sea to shining sea because it was a good free enterprise idea. He did not want to have a railway that ran from one end of this country to the other because an enormous profit could
be realized. He wanted a railway from sea to shining sea because he understood that in order to reconcile the differences between the various regions and people in this country he needed a way to unite them. The railroad was built from sea to sea, primarily from his initiative.
That is but one illustration of the role that transportation has always played in this country. Time does not permit me to give many other examples of the role of transportation in Canada.
Let us examine what has happened in the last couple of years. The Government has decided through its deregulation initiative that transportation is no longer an essential element of nation building. Furthermore, it has decided that transportation is no longer an essential ingredient in ensuring regional opportunities and regional equality. It has adopted a user fee policy in this country by which it implies that transportation facilities are no different from a McDonald's or a grocery store. Such stores are placed where there is enough demand and enough volume of sales. If you live in the tiniest town on the eastern shores of this great nation overlooking the Atlantic Ocean, there will be no McDonald's. According to the Government's user-pay policy, it is saying for the first time in our history that where there is a huge population and a demand, there will be transportation services.
Where there is not a huge population and where there is no market-place demand, where the free market sector will not give it, Government will no longer provide transportation services. That is a radical departure from Government policy in a country of 25 million people, a country which has within its boundaries the largest land mass, notwithstanding the Soviet Union, on the planet earth.
For the first time we are denying transportation services to the people who live in the province of my good friend, the Hon. Member for Egmont (Mr. Henderson), the Province of P.E.I., an island province. For those people the ferry system is not a scenic route by the sea. They do not wake up in the morning and say: "I think I will go out today and ride the ferry so I can enjoy the fresh air and the sunshine". They ride the damn ferry because there is no other way of moving themselves or freight onto or off that island. Yet the Government is now saying to P.E.I. that the ferry service shall be provided on a user-pay basis. There was a 15 per cent increase last year, and there were more increases announced last week, which means that ultimately we will essentially cut the umbilical cord, transportation, which keeps the island of P.E.I. viable and it will shrivel and die because the free market did not say that P.E.I. should live.
In my own Province of Newfoundland, which is separated from the rest of the country by 90 miles of water, that same kind of philosophy is applied with exactly the same kind of contemptible results. The Government wants to spend $600 million to build an ice-breaker to patrol our northern waters. Because the Government has such a friendly relationship with
October 31, 1986

the American administration, it now needs a $600 million monolith to keep the Americans from ploughing through our territorial waters. What is the best way of establishing one's ownership of something? What is the best way of proving one owns something? It is to be there, to have possession, and the way to demonstrate possession is not with a $600 million icebreaker. It is by supporting the people who live in the North, by giving them a transportation policy which allows them to live in the North and have a quality of life while they live there.
Rather than putting money into northern transportation systems, into getting rid of the high air fares for people who live in the North and allowing people to get goods, food and all the necessities of life at a reasonable cost so they will live in the North and hold up Canada's flag, we are going to put $600 million into an ice-breaker. That is the kind of irrational, knee-jerk, non-people oriented, free market balderdash being promoted by the Government.
There are a number of examples of the shortsighted doctrinaire and philosophical wizardry which this administration wants to impose upon the people of Canada. In Moncton, New Brunswick, a thousand jobs are now at stake because Canadian National-sea to shining sea-is no longer going to be a presence in New Brunswick. It is being moved out because the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) says he wants to get Candian National lean and mean and thinned out so he can privatize Canadian National.
A thousand jobs are going to disappear, but the answer of the Minster for Transport is that those people are no longer viable. I wrote down what he said. He said: "We are not going to dig rivers so we can build bridges". That begs the question. Is the Government going to manufacture prisoners to fill prisons? It cannot have it both ways.
The hypocrisy of the Government is appalling. It is not the hypocrisy that bothers me. It is not the fact that the Government talks out of both sides of its mouth that bothers me. It is not the fact that this kind of deception is being perpetrated that bothers me. It is the glibness with which the Government attempts this deception that bothers me. I do not mind having tall yarns spun but I mind very much when the person who is spinning those yarns has a grin on his face and actually believes that myself or the Canadian public is foolish enough to believe them. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, the people of Canada are not swallowing the double standards or, I should say, lack of standards of this administration.
The Canada Shipping Act was an Act which was in great need of overhaul. It desperately needed to be reviewed, modernized and updated. All of us in Parliament who are interested in transportation matters participated in that upgrading with Bill C-75. Members of all three Parties did a good job. But at the eleventh hour, the Minister of Transport of the day, the man who is currently Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), slipped in an innocuous sounding clause, Clause 4. I am sure Madam Speaker is beside herself wondering what is Clause 4. Why would it raise the ire of the Hon.

Member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe? Sit patiently, Madam Speaker, and I will tell you.
Clause 4 is a clause which allows the Minister of Transport to impose user-fees. "What for?", Madam Speaker asks, "What user-fees?" User-fees for Coast Guard services, navigational aids and ice-breaking services. Madam Speaker asks: "How can that be? We are a marine nation. We have the largest coastline of any nation on earth". Surely the Government of Canada would not contemplate telling people who are in need of search and rescue services that they have to think before they push the panic button because they may have to pay regardless of whether they can afford it. That is precisely what the Government is now attempting through Bill C-75.
That Bill died on the vine because we in the Liberal Party opposed it. We are now waiting to see how the new Minister of Transport, who comes from Newfoundland, feels. I would like to say of the Minister of Transport that he is an assembly line politician, body by Fisher and tongue by Gillette. I hope his brains are as sharp as his tongue and he will see the light of day and drop Clause 4. We are waiting for the answer with bated breath.
I issue a warning now that if Bill C-75 comes back to the House containing Clause 4, it will meet the most severe resistance this Party can mount to ensure that the little people of this country are not sacrificed.

You would not know about those kinds of people, the people who live in our towns and villages-

However, there is something desperately wrong when accompanying this idea of deregulation is the concept, as espoused by the Government and contained in the Bill, that transportation is no longer something born out of public necessity and convenience, as we have always defined it in Canada, but is instead something that is market-driven. There is something wrong when the Government says, for example in the case of airline transportation, that as of the date the new Bill is passed airlines will be able to enter and exit markets at will with only 60 days' notice to a regulatory agency and with no basis of appeal.
Let us try to understand what that means. Currently, airlines in the country are licensed on a route system. They are allowed to fly some of the money-paying routes, some of the gravy runs, but they must also by law take some of the lesser-paying routes in the rural and northern parts of Canada, both on the East Coast and in the western parts of Canada. By law they must, in financial terms, take some of the bad with the good. That is the way that we ensure that Canadians are given some minimal level of service no matter where they live.
Under the new legislation, airline companies will no longer be licensed on a route system. They will be licensed to fly to each and every individual stop in the land. If they want to abandon a northern community, they are required to give 60 days' notice and then they are out. There is no appeal possible or available to members of the local communities involved. There is no regulatory agency to pass judgment on what is a public necessity and convenience. If that is not treating the public's airways in the same fashion in which McDonald's treats it franchises, then I do not know what it is. The impact will be that in the far-flung regions of the country many of our citizens will be left with a third, fourth and fifth-rate service, or no service at all. That is the nature of deregulation.
With respect to the air side, we know that in the United States deregulation has led to huge losses and bankruptcies. Finally, it has led to mergers. Instead of a competitive environment, we are ending up with an industry which is more monopolistic than ever before and which is deeply in debt. That is the model that Canada is following. We know that in the first six months of this year CP Air has already lost $26.5 million. We know that in the first quarter of 1986 Air Canada has already lost $46.2 million. We know that Pacific Western has already lost $4.6 million in its first quarter. We know that every major company is losing money.
In that environment this administration wants to impose a U.S. model. I can only say this. If the user-pay philosophy continues, then the people of Canada will not have it. They can stand, in the interest of deficit-cutting, having a bit of fat cut. In the interest of deficit-cutting they can stand having a bit of muscle cut. But what they cannot stand is when the Government cuts through the fat, the muscle and down into the bone and begins to bleed away the marrow which is the life-blood of Canada.
It is time for the Government to wake up, conduct a complete review of its transportation policy in order to understand what it is doing to people who live in areas where the primary resources are produced. The Government must get back on an intelligent, compassionate and Canadian track, the kind of track proposed by John A. Macdonald, someone whom members of this Government claim to revere.

First,
Madam Speaker, I should like to comment briefly on the debates heard in the House earlier this morning and this afternoon. Considering all the speeches we got from the Opposition benches, NDP or Liberal, and everything we have experienced in this country in the last 25 years, I think we simply have to say that if this country has transportation problems in 1986, as we do back home in the Gaspe area and the Magdalen Islands, we owe them to others, and particularly to the Liberal Party.
Ever since September 4, 1984, Madam Speaker, we have tried with the former Minister and the new Minister of Transport to solve the problems about which Members of the Opposition failed to do anything at all during at least two decades. This is why we were enthusiastic about the National Transportation Act, Bill C-75 or any other. Transportation is the kind of issue which this Opposition did not want to tackle when they were on the Government side because they did not have enough courage. Indeed, Madam Speaker, prior to 1984 the previous Government had one principle, which was to stay in office. Do nothing, but hang on to power. We have no such principle, Madam Speaker. We are quite prepared to tackle these problems so that our fellow Canadians back home will be able to travel out of the Gaspe area just as easily as the people of Edmonton in Alberta, Newfoudland or anywhere else can travel from their place of residence. That is the problem we had to face in 1984. Regardless of the oratorical circumlocutions of our colleague from Newfoundland, our former Minister of Transport did not have the nerve to come to grips with transportation issues. Madam Speaker, the motion indicates that the Government has not been very active when it comes to airports. I should like to set straight our actions with regard to

airports. However, I should like to establish some background; to talk about the importance of airports; and to talk about Government actions in this regard, recommendations which have been made, and what the future might hold.
I will proceed by giving a little background for Hon. Members opposite. By way of profile, Transport Canada is involved with 213 airports across the country through direct ownership, operation, or financial support. Some 77 of the largest and busiest airports are operated and managed by the Department. Approximately $51 million has been invested, with 51 million deplaning and emplaning every year and with 4 million landings. It is a huge area of activity.
The capital value of investment in our airport facilities excluding land was $8 billion, and the revenues generated were around $600 million. Capital expenditures amounted to $214 million, and maintenance costs amounted to $398 million. We even found time to spend $36 million on non-federal airports. One can see that there has been a tremendous scope of activity with regard to airports in Canada. Indeed it is very important.
In addition to the approximate 4,500 employees, there are 500 Corps of Commissionaires and 400 RCMP officers. The retention of the RCMP was a major commitment of the Government to airport security. The Canadian airport system is recognized throughout the world as a leader in safety, security, and technology. Transport Canada is second only to the Soviet Union as the world's largest manager and operator of airports.
The contribution of airport activity to the national economy is significant. Airports are the focal point for regional and local economic activity resulting from direct expenditures by the airport aviation industry and associated commercial services, tourism, related transportation industries, and from many other direct and indirect expenditures.
In May, 1985 our Government initiated for consideration a new management structure for the federal airport system, one which would provide for a self-sustaining system and allow for the independent operation of local airports. That position was enhanced in June, 1985 with a position paper entitled Freedom to Move. The paper indicated that the Department of Transport would make every effort consistent with safety and security requirements to reduce the administrative burden of its operations, to ensure that existing facilities were being efficiently used before new capital expenditures were made, and to conduct operations and activities in a more commercial manner.
Hon. Members opposite indicated that we had no concern for the safety of Canadians, that we were sloughing off. I hope that I have made two points in what I have outlined thus far- first, that the Government has a tremendous commitment to the entire scope of airports in Canada and, second, that even though we want to look at new ways to manage the enterprise-and we are embarking upon those new ways-at no time has the safety of Canadians and indeed citizens of the world ever been given anything but the highest consideration.
