In October, 1985 a task force on airports was established. Its goals were to examine alternatives to the present management structure of Canada's airports and to take the first step in a consultative process designed to gather informed opinion on the subject. The task force was comprised of individuals from industry, the community, and Government. The task force report entitled The Future of Canadian Airport Management was released by the Minister of Transport as a basis for discussion with key groups and interested individuals as we continue to explore options for an improved airport management structure.
1 refer Hon. Members to some of the basic principles which the task force concluded were essential to ensure the wellbeing of Canada and Canadians under any new system and therefore, were necessary elements of any future management scheme for Canada's airports. The safety and security of the flying public and the airport property will remain paramount. I think it is important to reinforce that. The provision and operation of air navigation services, such as air traffic control, and of regulatory services, such as certification and enforcement, will continue to be the responsibility of the federal Government. As our task force travelled across Canada, we listened to Canadians from coast to coast who were concerned about those two items. We indicated-and certainly the task force report reveals it-that the Government was committed to the safety of the travelling public.
Transport Canada will maintain a national airport system plan. Any transfers should be subject to negotiations on a commercial basis. Any new owners shall have the freedom to design, construct, and operate site facilities provided that they adhere to the safety and security regulations. Finally, in the case of an imposed public duty not directly related to a commercial operation of an airport, new owners or operators shall be reimbursed for the related costs.
With those principles clearly before it, the task force went about its study and concluded by making the following recommendations to the Minister of Transport:
1.	retain the responsibility for safety and security within Transport Canada and ensure that the present high standards are not jeopardized.
2.	retain the responsibility for air navigation, air regulation and certification of airports within Transport Canada as a separate entity from airport management.
3.	be receptive to the establishment of local authorities by responding favourably to requests from local groups that have the support of their respective provincial and municipal levels of government.
4.	ensure that, where no immediate local interest exists to establish authorities, airports are transferred to Crown corporations.
5.	facilitate the changes already under way in Transport Canada to streamline the operation of airports and increase their commercial orientation.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) intends to use the task force report as a basis of further consultation. He has urged that this consultation procedure be a very active one. In my area of London-Middlesex some action is already under way. The municipal governments and the Chambers of
Commerce have committees in place and they are proposing recommendations to the Minister. I am sure that this is happening all over Canada. When given the opportunity to react to the recommendations of this task force, there are many Canadians interested in this new venture to revitalize the airports of Canada, and their recommendations will be coming forward to the Minister.
Safety and security continue as the highest priority within Transport Canada. The October 1 national security enhancement procedures for passengers and baggage have already been implemented. At the local level at the airport in London-Middlesex, over $200,000 has been spent on new security systems to make sure that passengers can travel without fear. New fencing systems have been put into that airport, as they have across Canada. Our record is impeccable.
Expo 86, the most successful world exposition in history, proceeded free of incident at the Vancouver International Airport. The same priority is being given to the preparation for the 1988 Olympics in Calgary.
The management of airports has been separated from the regulatory and navigational services within Transport Canada since October, 1985. One of the mandates given to the airport authority group in Transport Canada is to increase the commercial viability of airports and to close the gap between airport costs and airport revenues. A number of major thrusts are under way to stimulate revenue generation and encourage cost reduction with the overriding objective of having airports operated on a more business-like basis. Many local groups supported by the provincial and municipal governments have expressed interest in becoming more involved in the operation and promotion of their airports. This type of activity is alive and well in my part of Canada.
It was the Progressive Conservative Government that established the Montreal Airports Advisory Board and asked for local input to the resolution of the Mirabel-Dorval airports issue.
Representatives from all interested groups in the industry, business community, and provincial and municipal governments were brought together to make recommedations to the Minister of Transport.
Recent statements by the Government of British Columbia attest to their appreciation of the importance of airports to local and regional economies.
Local participation in the management of airports would promote not only the operations of the airports, but also the needs of local public and businesses, and permit greater potential for realization of private sector opportunities. That is one of the exciting new venues in airport development that will take place. The Minister of Transport recently announced the Department's intention to seek private sector investment in a third terminal at the country's busiest airport in Toronto.
The objective is to achieve a solution to the overcrowding of passenger processing facilities by getting the maximum

involvement of the private sector's innovation, entrepreneurial initiative, and commercial experience. The Department expects that this challenge will be accepted and that a new era of co-operation and partnership between the public and private sectors in the airport activity will be launched.
All the foregoing initiatives represent a reasoned, sensitive approach to seeking improvements in the management of the Canadian airport system. All these initiatives are being taken with full recognition of some basic principles. This is worth being repeated so that Members opposite and all Canadians will realize that safety and security are paramount. They are paramount in all of our planning on this side of the House and with our Minister of Transport. Our actions in the past two years have indicated our deepest concerns for this. In an era of world-wide terrorism and fear for the flying public, Canada has moved forward with new innovations in safety and new procedures for passengers and their baggage. We are internationally recognized for our achievements.
Better ways of operating the system are being sought while ensuring that equity of access is guaranteed and that a national system is maintained. There has been much talk that this Government will allow a fragmentation of the airport system of Canada. The point may certainly be made here today that we are going to maintain that national system of airports that we are so proud of. Indeed, we are recognized around the world as being a leader in the airport system.
Airports are an integral part of the Canadian economic fabric. Airports are essential for social transportation needs such as medical evacuation, resupply depots, and relief from isolation. When the standing committee travelled to the far north of Canada, we learned first-hand how important transportation is to the people who live north of 60'/3. We listened to them, and I hope we listened to them well. The Government is going to ensure access for those people to the south, and for them to visit their friends, relatives, business associates in the North. The Government is proceeding with the utmost regard for the economic and social well-being of all Canadians in its review of the airports system.
I think it is important that we say that airports have been vital to the development of Canada. Airports are today what railways were in an earlier time. Our Government recognizes that. We are committed to the development of new innovations in airports. I have cited one or two of them here today, our move to the private sector of terminal 3 in Toronto. There are other initiatives underway which will be reported to the Minister as a result of his task force on airports. The future bodes well for airport development and Canadians should know that this Government is committed to improving that service for all of us.

I want to concentrate a number of remarks in this area. First, there is the question of the policy of both the Liberals and the Conservatives on deregulation. We have always opposed this policy for a number of reasons, not the least of which is that it undermines services to less populated regions of Canada. It also undermines jobs, particularly women's jobs. It should be thoroughly evident to Members shouting across the aisle that the whole process of deregulation throws the airlines, particularly Canadian-owned airlines such as Air Canada, into cut-throat competition. As we know, larger airlines like Air Canada or CP Air tend to use regional carriers for other routes.
I think we will find that the airlines, in order to be competitive under this new regime, will cut back on expenses. The main expense they will cut back on is staff. I would like to point out that it is particularly women's jobs which are at great risk. As usual, women in the service type of position, such as flight attendants, ticket takers and maintenance staff are the ones most likely to be affected. I recall last year hearing from some women connected with airlines in the interior of B.C., for example, who were being forced to either lose their jobs or move as massive changes were occurring in their industry.
A couple of Members on the Government side mentioned that there was no concern about safety at Canadian airports under deregulation. The Canadian Aviation Safety Board apparently disagrees with this position. A recent clipping from The Globe and Mail said that more rest for flight crews is urged. Canada needs to radically strengthen regulations proposed for January to control flight crew fatigue in the country's sky. No other nation is as lenient in its regulations, the CASB said in a report to the Minister of Transport. There we have the view of flight crews who surely are in a position to know.
As to security at airports, I would like to remind Government Members, and the last speaker in particular, that the Government was committed to removing RCMP from airports. It was our Party which questioned this very strongly. As a result, the Minister reconsidered, after the Air India disaster, and we finally got a decision to keep the RCMP in supervisory positions at airports. Having said that, I would like to use my time primarily to concentrate on transportation issues and policies which have come to my attention over the last year or two as a result of my contacts as the Member of Parliament for Vancouver East. Our concern primarily was shipping and shipping-related industries, and the Port of Vancouver. What happens to the Port of Vancouver, of course, reflects what is happening to the West Coast generally.
First of all, we were concerned and continue to be concerned that Bill C-25 provided for increased charges for Coast Guard services or use of Government wharves and other services. We continue to be concerned that such charges will increase the cost of shipping. It is already difficult to compete in the shipping business and this will make us less competitive. This is of great concern and could be a considerable burden on smaller boat owners, and operators of fishing vessels.
I want to raise another point which has come to our attention. I believe it was the Liberals who terminated the weather ships off the West Coast. I know people who worked on those ships and it was very important that we had them off the coast to warn small boat owners of coming storms, as well as providing marine research services. Now we have the threat that lighthouse keepers off the B.C. coast will be replaced by computers. I would just like to point out, if Members do not already know, that lighthouse keepers do much more than turn on lights.
I have a very strong letter from the United Fishermen and Allied Workers on this issue. They are very concerned that the Department of Transport plans to do away with the manning of seven lighthouses and cut staff by half or more in five others. These lighthouse keepers play a vital role in helping to make the waters off the B.C. coast safer for mariners, both commercial and pleasure. There have been numerous cases where lighthouse keepers have saved the lives of fishermen when their boats floundered. Many other cases go unreported where, by way of a timely bit of information about the weather, a boat and the lives of the crew are saved.
The waters off the B.C. coast are among the most dangerous in the world. Seven fishermen have died since the first of the year. Lighthouse keepers are an integral part of the already too-thinly stretched safety web on this coast, so we appeal to the Government to reconsider and make sure that the lighthouse keeping service is preserved.
My concerns, as I said, are particularly related to other matters affecting the Port of Vancouver and other West Coast ports. First of all, I would like to point out that we heard earlier this year about the rather insidious trend developing, and there was no Government intervention at all to prevent this, whereby shipping from Central Canada to the West Coast and from there to ships to go across the Pacific Rim is deliberately being cultivated along U.S. routes rather than
Canadian routes. I refer particularly to CN which I understand has increasingly been using routes which connect from Central Canada down to Chicago, from there across American railways, and from there through the Port of Seattle or other West Coast American ports rather than Canadian ports.
These are Canadian goods leaving Canada or coming to Canada. I think that is a disgraceful situation. There are a number of reasons for this. I understand that the U.S. has favourable tariffs to encourage this. They also have double decker carriers for containers. These are problems that we should be looking into in Canada and, if necessary, we should improve our technology. However, we should have some kind of intervention by the Government which prevents a Crown corporation from shipping Canadian goods through the United States and out through American ports rather than on Canadian railways through Canadian ports.
I would also like to talk about other issues such as a current concern which I raised this week with the Minister of Labour (Mr. Cadieux) about the Port of Vancouver and the fact that longshoremen were locked out by the Maritime Employers Council and the tremendous danger this is to the shipment of grain and other cargo out of the Port of Vancouver.
I was very pleased when New Democratic Members raised this in the House. Several weeks ago the Minister intervened and the employers' council agreed to a 30-day cooling off period. The lock-out provision was withdrawn, the people went back to work and the grain was allowed to flow through the Port of Vancouver. It was very upsetting to learn this week that, although there were nine days left in the 30-day cooling off period, the employers had stopped negotiating. On Monday the Minister said that he would intervene once again. We certainly hope that he will and that these disputes can be resolved in order to allow shipping to continue through the Port of Vancouver. The union has assured us that grain and bulk cargo will continue to be handled if there should be a lock-out. However, we want to prevent a lock-out.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak to the motion standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet). This motion not only concerns transportation and the difficulties in that sector, it relates to the general policies of the Government with regard to regional development.
When the Government came to office two years ago, it seemed to adopt a trickle-down approach by which it would make the successful areas of our country grow rapidly so that eventually some benefits would trickle down to the outlying regions of our country. The Government pursued this policy for almost two years, until the uproar in its caucus was so incredible that it abandoned that policy last July 7.
In fact, in the Speech from the Throne the Government for the first time talked about an economic opportunities council in Atlantic Canada and diversifying the economy in western Canada. It is interesting for Liberal, Conservative and New Democrat Members from northern Ontario to note that the Throne Speech did not say anything about setting up an economic diversification council or anything else for nothern Ontario.
Perhaps if the Government's other policies were successful, it may have had an opportunity to let the trickle-down theory work. It has been said that if one feeds the horse enough oats, the sparrows will have some. Obviously the screams from the sparrows in the Tory caucus from Atlantic Canada, western Canada, and northern Ontario became unbearable for the
Cabinet because when it met in Saskatoon in the first week of July, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) suddenly discovered regional development. In the meantime, however, he had drastically reduced the budget of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and reduced subsidies for transportation and other programs in eastern Canada.
The Prime Minister launched a privatization program which may be quite successful in Toronto and the Golden Horseshoe, but does not do much for the regions of the country. That background and the introduction of the privatization legislation during the last gasp of the last session in June has led to this debate on transportation policy today.
This debate is very appropriate because it allows Members on all sides to describe how the transportation policies and general approach of the Government with regard to privatization is working. In terms of general economic growth in the regions of the country, I am suggesting that the Government's general economic policies have not been successful. Clearly, between 1983 and 1986, under both Governments, we have seen a dramatic 3.5 per cent to 4.5 per cent growth in the southern Ontario area, but I contend that the growth in the regions of our country, whether we are talking about forestry, or mining in northern Ontario, has not been spectacular.
This is particularly true in the energy field. The former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister for International Trade (Miss Carney), said that she would create hundreds of thousands of jobs in the energy sector. We can see that at least 55,000 jobs have been lost in the energy sector alone.

Madam Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity to respond to the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Lesick) in terms of transportation. Clearly, the Government of the Hon. Member when it came to power talked about allowing free market forces to decide everything. Under the present Government we were supposed to really see the economy grow. There was supposed to be a natural development in all regions of the country without any direction or assistance from the Government. Clearly, if one travels around Canada today and looks at the policies of Government in Atlantic Canada, in particular, one will see that there are user fees. Where there has been a reduction of assistance for transportation, one will see very concerned regions of the country. I doubt that most regions of the country, apart from the Golden Horseshoe of Toronto and its environs, are really seeing much growth at all, probably not even 1 per cent or 2 per cent. Clearly in the mining areas of the country there does not seem to be any policy for development.

Well, if he were to talk to the Air Canada workers who were in Sault Ste Marie earning $13.50 per hour three weeks ago and who are now trying to feed their families on the $6.50 per hour they earn at Shell, then he would clearly see that the Government's policies concerning deregulation and pulling out of Air Canada are not very convincing. If the Hon. Member were living in the community of Wawa and working for Algoma Ore Properties and if he were to hear the Government saying that, well, its policy is survival of the fittest, then he would wonder whether there would be any existing jobs.
I think the fact that the Government tried its policies for two years, saw that it was disastrous in the energy sector, saw that its whole thrust in free trade has been fraught with difficulties and is likely to collapse over the next year, then he would understand that when the Prime Minister came out of the cabinet meeting in Saskatoon last summer he was not talking so much about free market sources but about regional development as if he had just discovered it. In the Speech from the Throne the Prime Minister talked about an Atlantic Canada Opportunity Agency and then he talked about regional diversification in western Canada. This did not happen because he had a divine inspiration. It happened because back-benchers were screaming loud and clear every Wednesday morning.
Suddenly, the cabinet Ministers were screaming loud and clear in Saskatoon. Suddenly, regional policies concerning transporation and other issues were giving a new aspect to the Government's policy. The Hon. Member talks about there being no constraints on transportation and the general economy being freed-up. In many areas the general economy has not only been freed-up, it is not growing at all.
I hope the Government will get concerned about how transportation relates to those regions because transportation

is a vital instrument and part of the regional development policy in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Kilgour (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in view of the transportation policies implemented by the Liberals, I consider this motion to be a bad Halloween trick. For instance, just before the 1984 elections, when the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) was Minister of Transport, he had a staff of 127 officials, and believe it or not, the now Deputy Prime Minister reduced this number to 30. As a second example, there were the cutbacks made to VIA Rail services under the Liberals in 1981, I believe, and the fact that we re-established those services. In other words, we have no lesson to learn from the Liberals in the area of transport.

Time is limited and I have much to say. I will have to go quite quickly.
In reply to the motion before the House, I would like to speak on Freedom to Move, the Government's plan for economic regulatory reform in transportation. Please note that I did not say deregulation. We have only made plans for regulatory reform. In some cases, there will be much less regulation; in some cases, more; in all cases, better regulation. We are not simply following models in other countries by deregulating everthing.
As I said earlier, we plan to have more regulation in some cases, particularly regarding safety. I would point out 13,000 person-years are involved in safety programs on which $1.2 billion is being spent. Many of these programs will expand because safety was, is and always will be the prime issue of importance to the Government.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
We do believe that the existing regulatory regime needs to be improved. The transportation system must be run for the long-term good of all Canadians. The regulatory regime must be open and responsive to the needs of Canadians from St. John's to Nanaimo. We will have a made-in-Canada policy, recognizing Canada's unique characteristics and transportation requirements.
The policy has been refined through extensive consultations with business, transportation companies, users, labour, the travelling public and provincial and territorial Governments. The main thrust of it will be to bring economic reform to transportation in Canada, to encourage competition, to improve the price and range of transportation services and to support the growth of key economic sectors in society. For once, the tilt will be in favour of consumers, not the shippers and transportation companies.
If I may, I would like to give the House a summary of how Freedom to Move came about. For at least five years and in some cases 10 or more years, various groups and inquiries have
Supply
suggested that Canada's regulatory policy and process should be modified and updated to fit in with the late 20th century. For example, the Economic Council of Canada, university transportation centres, shippers' and consumer groups, government studies and various consultants have frequently documented the case for less regulation in air; different, more uniform and less regulation in trucking; improved, speedier and fairer regulations for rail shippers and especially for captive shippers; and a leaner regulatory agency with a capacity for faster and fairer regulation. These and other pressures including ones from south of the border have led many to the conclusion that we should undertake not a piecemeal but a comprehensive reform package.
The then Minister of Transport, the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), officially introduced the idea of comprehensive regulatory reform in a speech he made to the Canadian Industrial Traffic League in February, 1985. He suggested that all regulatory legislation ought to be updated and modified at about the same time and within the same framework. There was a country-wide process of meetings, discussions and consultations and the inquiry got under way immediately.
The rationale and the basic elements for regulatory reform were introduced in a document entitled Freedom to Move in July, 1985. Once again, there was extensive consultation with all on many occasions. Where the feedback was persuasive, several modifications to the proposals have been made. Such modifications have been made in northern air travel, trucking regulation and the recognition of a legislative link between transportation and regional economic development.

The Hon. Member for Bonaventure-iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Gray) spoke about this basic question this afternoon and we recognized this point of which many have already spoken.

The proposed Transportation Act and Motor Vehicle Transport Act were introduced in Parliament on June 26 as Bills C-126 and C-127. With the proroguing of the House of Commons, those two Bills died on the Order Paper. The legislation has been accorded the highest priority by Cabinet and I am happy to announce that the two Bills will be reintroduced to the House of Commons on a priority basis next week.
The four main components of the legislation on which I will touch today if there is time are air, rail, trucking and marine. I will deal with aviation First.
Those of us in southern Canada have been receiving the benefits of a reformed and less extensive regulatory environment in the air industry for a number of years. This has come about by various Ministerial policies and by Canadian Transport Commission regulatory changes on entry and exit rulings, tariffs and licensing conditions. Freedom to Move actually brings the legislation more into conformity with the way the southern Canada air transportation environment

October 31, 1986
Supply
currently operates and at the same time eliminates much of the existing obsolete and unnecessary regulatory authority. The obvious general support given to the adoption of the principles of Freedom to Move relative to all air services in southern Canada proves the point.
The actual reform proposals for the airline sector in 1985 were the following: first, entry to any class of domestic commercial air service would be based on a "fit, willing and able" requirement as opposed to the current public convenience and necessity test. Again, it is the consumer we are trying to help, not the carriers. Compliance with the Ministry of Transport's safety regulations-and the Minister has constantly said that this is our first concern-for operating certification and proof of adequate insurance coverage with be required to meet the new entry requirement. Second, withdrawal would not be impeded except by a requirement for advance notice. Third, there would be no ongoing regulation of domestic tariffs but there would be provisions for the agency to review unreasonable fare increases. Carriers would be required to make their schedules of tariffs and tolls available at their business offices for public information purposes and to retain a record of such tariffs and tolls for a minimum of three years but would not be required to file them with the new regulatory agency which would replace the CTC.
These regulations were originally intended to cover all of Canada but that most invaluable tool, the consultation process, came into play. We received many submissions on regulatory reform as it applied to northern air transport including submissions from the Governments of Yukon and NWT. Travellers, shippers, communities and individual carriers all made their views known.
Three major reports indicated that air services to northern and remote areas were essential. We accept that. The areas are sparsely populated with small communities, meaning small markets. Carriers depend upon a mix of passenger and freight to remain viable. Charter operations make up a significant proportion of revenues. Freight flow is unidirectional, meaning that freight revenue must also cover return trip costs. It is more expensive to operate in the North, as we know, and traffic is very seasonal with less prosperous times during large parts of the year.
All these factors had an influence upon government thinking. They told us that for now, and for a considerable time to come, some degree of economic regulation was needed to ensure the stability and adequacy of air services in the North. They also made us realize that the immediate application of the fit, willing and able entry standard may not provide enough regulation to ensure the goals of adequacy and stability.
At the same time, maintaining the status quo is simply not a tenable proposition. It is unduly bureaucratic. The regulatory burden is too heavy. It limits the ability to serve markets
efficiently. It is not always responsive to needs, and it means higher prices for the often neglected consumer.
A new modified regulatory reform initiative is proposed for air services to, from, and within northern Canada. It is designed to assist the transition of carriers into a more competitive environment, to be sufficiently flexible, and to gradually bring the benefits of increased competition to northern travellers and shippers.
The key aspects of this modified regulatory regime are as follows. First, applicants who wish to start a new air service will be required to meet the safety and insurance requirements. There will be a new reverse onus public interest entry test whereby entry would be granted unless those opposing the application can establish, to the satisfaction of the new regulatory agency, that allowing such entry would lead to a serious decrease in the level of air services provided at regulated communities, or would create significant instability in the provision of essential air services at protected communities. There would be a more pro-competitive entry test than the current public convenience and necessity test.
Licence conditions will continue in the North to limit aspects of the activities of carriers such as the type of service- scheduled versus charter-routes, points to be served, and schedules. Anyone wishing to leave a market would only have to give 60 days notice to the agency. There would be no requirement to maintain service beyond the notice period.
As for southern Canada, tariffs in the North will no longer have to be filed with the agency but simply maintained at their business offices for public inspection and kept for a period of three years to comply with potential agency needs. Unreasonable fare levels and increases will be reviewable upon complaint, and confidential contracts will be allowed. No subsidy program is intended, but the Minister will have the authority to grant a subsidy in cases of urgent necessity.
I should now like to turn briefly to the subject of rail transportation where we will again have a mixture of regulatory reform. In some cases it will be less; in several cases it will be more. The new legislation will allow shippers to negotiate confidential contracts with Canadian railways for the first time. Shippers and railways will have the flexibility to negotiate the services and other conditions appropriate to a shipper's circumstance and to tailor rates more closely to the competitive situation of the shipper. To protect against abuse, confidential contracts will be filed with the agency, and summaries of the non-confidential components will be published.
The existing provisions on agreed charges, which are essentially open public contracts, are continued in the new National Transportation Act primarily as a transition measure since a number of shippers currently benefit from them.
In the interest of fair competition between railways and between truckers and railways, the new legislation retains the essential requirement that all rates be compensatory. Modifications will focus on the prohibition of rates which are
October 31, 1986

predatory-and we in western Canada know about those-or designed to drive a competitor from the market.
These changes affecting rail freight tariffs will allow shippers and railways more freedom to adopt a commercially innovative approach to rate and service negotiations. Shippers will benefit from specially negotiated rates and conditions which reflect their own particular situations. Railways will be in a position to compete effectively with U.S. railways for transborder traffic. That is a very important factor today. The role of the new agency will be that of a watch-dog, acting only on complaints.
The new legislation also zeroes in on what has been described as Canada's No. 1 transportation problem-the captive shipper. Captive shippers fall into two general categories. To some extent they can be found in major metropolitan centres on the lines of a single railway carrier but beyond the four-mile interswitching limit, such as major oil refineries in the Montreal and Toronto areas.
Captive shippers may also be those resource shippers located in the more northern or remote areas of the Atlantic provinces, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba, and certainly in various parts of Alberta, Saskatchewan, and British Columbia. They are essentially captive to one railway without the possibility of enjoying a real, practical, and cost effective choice of either intermodal or intramodal transportation to move their lumber, coal, potash, or other mineral or petrochemical products.
Our Freedom to Move legislation will get at the heart of these problems by introducing competitive line rates, terminal running rights, and increased interswitching. They are all designed to give the captive shipper a competitive option and to provide competition through regulation.
I should like to make three main points. Competitive line rates is a fairly simple concept. Captive shippers who are local to just one carrier will be able to have access to another carrier at the closest interchange. This means that captive shippers will have competitive options, services, routes, and very likely competitive rates. This is something which they do not enjoy under current legislation. It is something about which we in western Canada have been shrieking politely for many years.
Competitive line rates will only be available to those shippers who cannot benefit from the new interswitching limits or from terminal running rights. Also, the common carrier responsibility will be on the connecting carrier, not the originating one.
Supply
I should point out that this will not necessarily result in short hauling or a diversion away from the local carrier. It will result in that situation only where the local carrier cannot or refuses to respond to or match the competitive rate being offered by the other carrier. As in any other industry, it is only lack of competitiveness which may result in traffic loss over a part of the route to destination. For domestic movements, including import and export traffic at Canadian ports, shippers will have to designate a continuous Canadian route if more than one continuous, cost effective Canadian route exists. This is designed to protect domestic traffic for Canadian railway carriers.
Shippers have embraced this concept as an answer to their problems. It is supported by the CMA, CITL, Coal Association of Canada, Canadian Fertilizer Institute, Council of Forest Industries, Canadian Pulp and Paper Association, Retail Council of Canada, Grocery Products Manufacturers of Canada, Mining Association of Canada, Propane Gas Association of Canada, Canadian Chemical Producers Association, and several others. These groups represent billions of dollars in railway freight rate revenue annually.
Despite objections from CN, CP, and several labour unions, we think that with the conditions attached to competitive line rates, this proposal will not seriously affect their returns. We also recognize that we must allow the railways to reduce their costs, that is, more freedom to manage their affairs with fewer legislative and regulatory hurdles.?
The second measure designed to increase competitive access for captive shippers is the issue of terminal running rights. Originally proposed by CP Rail, it will allow one railway to run over the lines of another railway within a 50-kilometre radius of a railway interchange.
The third measure will substantially increase the present four-mile limit for railway car interswitching in urban areas to 30 kilometres. Canadian cities have grown rapidly, and the limit should reflect today's realities. Flowever, the new interswitching charges will have to be compensatory.

It being five o'clock, it is my duty to inform the House that pursuant to Standing Order 82(12) the proceedings on the motion have expired.
Accordingly the House stands adjourned until eleven o'clock a.m. pursuant to Standing Order 3(1).

The House adjourned at 5 p.m.

*
Monday, November 3, 1986
